judge_panel.reason: The paper's own Sec. 4.2 honestly explains that the single k=6, a+5b exception is an "optimisation artefact" that "resolves to INST under longer training," and Table 2 shows that the failure was at one seed only (20/21 seeds succeeded). The abstract's claim of "no memorisation regime" refers to non-representable tasks, not to representable ones with slow convergence, and the 99.8% figure is explicitly tied to the 585-run dataset—the paper never claims all runs converge identically under the fast budget.

Section 4.2 does report one optimisation exception—“At k = 6 the rate drops to 95% (20/21 seeds), with the single exception being the task a + 5b at one seed... the shortfall was a transient optimisation issue”—but it is not a memorisation regime counterexample. The paper also states: “there are no MEM outcomes and no GROK outcomes... Every run lands in exactly one of the two extreme categories,” so the flagged claim incorrectly treats a transient FAIL-vs-INST optimisation miss as evidence against the ‘no memorisation regime’ conclusion.

The reviewer incorrectly conflates a transient optimization failure on a representable task with a 'memorisation regime'. The paper explicitly addresses this exception as a "transient optimisation issue" and confirms that across all runs "there are no MEM outcomes and no GROK outcomes."
